title: My head hurts — sentences that flip the subject
goal: Say what hurts, and get by at the pharmacy and the doctor's — while learning a sentence pattern that flips your way of thinking: it isn't you who aches, it's your body part, and you're the target.
bekal: naming body parts and using *Boli me …* / *Bolijo me …*
using the dative for states: *Slabo mi je*, *Vroče mi je*, *Všeč mi je*
getting by at the pharmacy: describing symptoms, asking for medicine, understanding advice

dialogs.title: Dialogue — Pri zdravnici
dialogs.intro: Budi goes to the campus clinic with a throat that feels like sandpaper. The doctor explains more than he asked.

lines.speaker: Budi:
lines.id: My head hurts. And my throat.

lines.speaker: Budi:
lines.text: Zakaj rečete boli me, ne jaz bolim?
lines.id: Why do you say "boli me" and not "jaz bolim"?
lines.literal: why you-say hurts me-acc, not I I-hurt?

lines.speaker: Zdravnica:
lines.text: Ker glava boli. Vi ste tarča.
lines.id: Because your head is doing the hurting. You're the target.
lines.literal: because head hurts. you are target.

lines.speaker: Budi:
lines.text: Torej glava dela, jaz pa trpim.
lines.id: So my head does the work, and I do the suffering.
lines.literal: so head works, I but I-suffer.

lines.speaker: Zdravnica:
lines.text: Tako je. Pijte čaj in počivajte.
lines.id: That's right. Drink tea and get some rest.
lines.literal: so is. drink-imp tea and rest-imp.

notes: **Boli me glava is literally "head hurts me".** The body part is the **subject**, and you are the **object**. That's why the form used for you is the accusative (*tožilnik*): *me*, *te*, *ga*, *jo*, *nas*, *vas*, *jih*. Translating straight from English — *jaz bolim* — would mean "I hurt (someone else)".

**If the body part is plural, the verb goes plural too.** *Boli me glava* (one head) but *Bolijo me noge* (two legs), *Bolijo me oči*, *Bolijo me zobje*. Notice that for a pair of body parts Slovenian uses the plural, not the dual — an old habit that survives only here.

**Slabo mi je uses yet another form: the dative (*dajalnik*).** Compare: *Boli **me*** (direct object) but *Slabo **mi** je* (to me). Almost all physical states and feelings use *mi*: *Vroče mi je* (I'm hot), *Mrzlo mi je* (I'm cold), *Dolgčas mi je* (I'm bored).

**Body temperature is said without the word "point".** *Sedemintrideset devet* means 37.9. Slovenia uses Celsius, and the fever threshold people use at home is 37.5. Notice too that *vročina* means both fever and hot weather — context tells them apart.

**Pijte in počivajte — the polite command form.** The *-te* ending makes it polite and plural at the same time, just like ordinary verbs. To a friend: *Pij čaj in počivaj*. Commands are covered in full in unit 19; for now, just recognize the ending.

grammars.title: Boli me — the flipped sentence pattern
body: One pattern, and it covers every physical complaint you'll ever make. All that changes is the object pronoun and how many body parts there are.
after: The object pronoun is a clitic, so it sits in second place as usual: *Danes **me** boli glava*, *Že tri dni **me** boli grlo*.
To say how much it hurts: *Zelo me boli* (it really hurts), *Malo me boli* (it hurts a bit), *Ne boli me več* (it doesn't hurt anymore).

grammars.title: Dajalnik — the "to" form
body: This fourth case marks **to whom** something happens. At A1 you'll mostly meet it in pronouns, and almost always with a neuter adjective.
after: The *Všeč mi je* row is worth learning right now: this is how Slovenian says **I like**. Literally it's "it is pleasing to me", so the thing you like is the subject: *Všeč mi je ta knjiga* (I like this book), *Všeč si mi* (I like you). If what you like is plural, the verb follows: *Všeč so mi te knjige*.
*Žal mi je* means both "I'm sorry" and "what a pity" — it's used for sincere apologies and for turning things down gently: *Žal mi je, ne morem* (sorry, I can't).

blocks.text: The third column is the form you'll actually use in a *Boli me …* sentence, so learn that column rather than the dictionary form.
*Nos mi teče* is literally "nose runs to me" — the Slovenian way to say you have a runny nose. The dative pattern again, and once again the body part is the subject.

Notice **oko** → **oči** and **uho** → **ušesa**: two plurals that follow no rule at all, inherited from Old Slavic. Since eyes and ears always come in pairs, the singular is rarely used unless one of them is giving you trouble.

sections.title: At the pharmacy and the doctor's

blocks.text: A handful of sentences that cover almost every minor health matter — from describing symptoms to buying medicine.

head: Slovenščina
Say it
English
rows: Do you have anything for a headache?

blocks.text: The emergency numbers in Slovenia are **112** for ambulance and fire, **113** for police. Both work nationwide and are free from any phone.

blocks.title: What newcomers should know
items: A pharmacy is a **lekarna**, and almost all of them close at night. The ones open around the clock are called **dežurna lekarna**, and every town has at least one.

Many medicines sold over the counter in other countries — including antibiotics — need a **prescription** (*recept*) in Slovenia. Ordinary painkillers such as *lekadol* or *aspirin* can still be bought directly.
If you're staying long-term, you'll get a **kartica zdravstvenega zavarovanja** (health insurance card). Always carry it — without it, a doctor's visit is charged in full.

blocks.text: And one sentence you'll often hear as an answer: *Ni hudega* — "it's nothing serious". Together with *Bo že* (it'll get better), these are how Slovenians comfort someone who's ill: short, calm, no drama.
